one_liner: Physical and emotional symptoms in the days after stopping or sharply reducing an antidepressant, usually brief but sometimes severe.
in_simple_words: When an antidepressant is stopped suddenly or reduced too fast, some people get symptoms within a few days: dizziness, nausea, flu-like feelings, 'electric shock' sensations, vivid dreams, trouble sleeping, anxiety, and irritability. It's not addiction, and it's not the depression returning, though it can be confused with relapse. Symptoms are usually mild and pass within two weeks; for a smaller number they're severe or longer-lasting. Reducing slowly, in steps agreed with your prescriber, prevents or eases most of it.
what_it_can_feel_like: I thought I was relapsing. The dizziness and the brain zaps started three days after I ran out. My GP explained and we tapered properly.
Coming off took me a year of tiny steps. Slow was fine. Fast had been awful.
common_signs: Dizziness, nausea, headache, or flu-like feelings within days of stopping
Brief 'electric shock' sensations, often with eye or head movement
Vivid dreams, insomnia, anxiety, irritability, or low mood
Usually begins within a week and eases over one to two weeks
More likely with sudden stops and with certain antidepressants

myths_vs_facts.fact: Antidepressants don't cause craving or compulsive use. The body adjusts to them, so stopping needs to be gradual, which is different from addiction.

myths_vs_facts.myth: Symptoms after stopping mean you'll always need the medication.
myths_vs_facts.fact: Discontinuation symptoms are the body adjusting, not proof you need the drug. A slower taper usually resolves them. Relapse is a separate question to review with your prescriber.
A 2024 analysis found about 1 in 6 or 7 people get symptoms beyond placebo, and about 1 in 35 get severe symptoms. Most people stop without major difficulty.

how_common.plain: After accounting for placebo effects, roughly 1 in 6 to 7 people who stop an antidepressant get at least one discontinuation symptom, and about 1 in 35 get severe symptoms.
how_common.figure: About 15% with any symptom and about 3% with severe symptoms after adjusting for placebo; 31% unadjusted (Lancet Psychiatry meta-analysis, 2024)

what_helps.plain_summary: The main approach is prevention: when it's time to stop, reduce the dose gradually in steps, over weeks to months depending on the medication and the person, with your prescriber. If symptoms appear, going back to the previous dose and reducing more slowly usually settles them. Some medications may be switched to a longer-acting one to make tapering easier. The Royal College of Psychiatrists and NICE both recommend tapering and shared decisions. Never stop suddenly without advice.
evidence_based_options: Gradual dose reduction planned with your prescriber
Returning to the previous dose and tapering more slowly if symptoms appear
Switching to a longer-acting antidepressant to ease tapering, in some cases
Monitoring for relapse separately from discontinuation symptoms
self_help_that_supports_care: Not running out of medication; keep a supply during a taper
Tracking symptoms and mood so you and your prescriber can tell them apart
Choosing a calm period to taper, with support in place
Reading patient guidance from the Royal College of Psychiatrists or NICE

when_to_reach_out: If you want to stop an antidepressant, talk to your prescriber first and make a plan. If you've stopped and feel dizzy, sick, or strange, contact them; it's usually easy to fix. If your mood drops sharply or you have thoughts of ending your life, use the crisis strip now.
is_not: Depression or anxiety returning after stopping is relapse, not discontinuation; it tends to come later and build slowly. Side effects while taking the medication are a different issue. Stopping a benzodiazepine or opioid is withdrawal and needs its own medical plan.
hope_note: Most people come off antidepressants without serious trouble when it's done gradually. Slow is the whole trick.

content_notes: Site-wide crisis link stays one tap away.
No doses or tapering schedules given; always 'with your prescriber'.
